quote: Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.
firstReading: John sees an angel restrain the dragon, while those who remained faithful to Christ share in his reign. Then the dead stand before God’s throne and are judged according to what is recorded in the books. Death and the netherworld are finally overcome. God reveals a new heaven and a new earth, and the holy city, the new Jerusalem, descends from God, prepared as a bride.
psalmSummary: Psalm 84 voices a pilgrim’s desire for the dwelling place of the Lord. Even the birds find a home near God’s altar, while those who live in his house continually praise him. Blessed are those whose strength is in God and whose hearts are set upon the holy journey. The psalm asks God to hear and behold his people with favor.
gospelSummary: Jesus uses the budding fig tree to teach his disciples how to discern the nearness of God’s kingdom. Just as new leaves indicate the approach of summer, the events he has described show that God’s saving purpose is moving toward fulfillment. His words do not invite fearful calculation or speculation about dates. Rather, they summon believers to attentive faith, because the visible world is passing and Christ’s word remains permanently true. The disciples are to place their confidence in him amid every sign of upheaval.
saintReflection: Saint Vergilius of Salzburg (Commemoration): Saint Vergilius of Salzburg (d. 784), an Irish monk, became abbot of Saint Peter's monastery and later Bishop of Salzburg. He supported missionary work among Slavic peoples, encouraged learning, and contributed to the building of the cathedral in Salzburg. His life was marked by controversy with Saint Boniface over pastoral and theological questions, yet the Church venerates both men, reminding the faithful that saints may experience real disagreement while remaining servants of the same Gospel. Vergilius defended the universality of God's creation and salvation against narrow assumptions of his age. He invites humility in controversy, patience in ecclesial discernment, support for missionary communities, and confidence that faith and careful inquiry are ordered toward the one truth whose source is God.
dailyPrayer:
Lord Jesus Christ, your word endures when heaven and earth pass away. Steady my heart when I see confusion, suffering, division, or the frailty of all that seems secure. Grant me the faith to recognize that your kingdom is near, not as a cause for fear, but as the promise of your final victory over sin, death, and every power opposed to your love.

Teach me to long for your dwelling place as the psalmist does. Make my prayer a true pilgrimage toward you, and give me strength to worship you faithfully in your Church. Purify my deeds, for all things are open before your judgment seat; yet preserve me from despair, for you prepare a new creation for those redeemed by your mercy.

Through the intercession of Saint Vergilius of Salzburg, grant me humility amid disagreement, patience in discerning truth, and zeal for the proclamation of the Gospel among all peoples. May faith and careful inquiry lead me more deeply to you, the source of all truth. Amen.
theologicalSynthesis:
The readings join Christian hope to the final judgment and renewal of creation. Revelation does not present history as an endless cycle or as a realm abandoned to evil. The dragon’s power is limited, the dead are judged before God, and death itself is cast away. The final horizon is the new heaven, the new earth, and the holy city coming from God. Christian hope therefore rests in God’s just and merciful act of making all things new.

Psalm 84 gives this hope its ecclesial and liturgical form. The faithful do not await God’s future from a distance; they already seek his presence and praise him in his dwelling. In the Gospel, Jesus grounds such hope in the permanence of his own word. Created realities pass, but the Lord’s teaching and promise do not fail.

Saint Vergilius’s defense of the universality of creation and salvation harmonizes with this vision. The God who renews creation gathers peoples into one saving purpose. His example calls the Church to missionary charity, intellectual humility, and patient communion when difficult questions require discernment.
exegesis:
Context: The final days of the liturgical year direct the Church toward the consummation of history. Revelation and Luke both address realities that can unsettle the human heart: conflict, judgment, the passing of the present order, and the coming reign of God. Yet neither reading permits despair. Their purpose is to strengthen persevering faith. The Christian does not gaze upon the end merely as destruction, but as the revelation of God’s justice and the fulfillment of his saving promise. What is passing is not God’s goodness, nor Christ’s lordship, nor the communion God intends for his people.

First Reading: John’s vision portrays the dragon as subject to God’s command, not as an equal rival to him. The restraint of the deceiver and the reign of those faithful to Christ affirm that martyrdom and fidelity are not defeats. The vision then turns to the great judgment. The dead stand before God, and their deeds are disclosed. This is morally serious: human acts belong before the truth of God. But the passage reaches beyond judgment to promise. Death and the netherworld themselves are overcome, and John sees a new heaven, a new earth, and the new Jerusalem. God’s final purpose is not abandonment of creation but its renewal.

Psalm: Psalm 84 answers Revelation’s vision with the prayer of a pilgrim who desires God’s dwelling. The psalmist’s longing is not escape from the world, but a desire to abide where God is worshiped and praised. Even the small creatures near the altar become signs of the security found in God’s presence. Those whose strength is in the Lord are blessed because their journey is directed toward him. In the light of Revelation, this pilgrimage also bears an ultimate meaning: the Church moves toward the holy city that comes from God. Worship forms the faithful for that destiny by teaching them to seek God above all passing goods.

Gospel: Jesus’ image of the fig tree calls for spiritual attentiveness. Its leaves do not enable someone to control summer; they simply reveal that summer is near. Likewise, the events Jesus describes are signs that history is moving under God’s providence toward fulfillment. The disciples are not given permission to construct anxious predictions. They are taught to recognize the approach of God’s kingdom and to remain faithful. Christ then sets his own word above the instability of the created order. Heaven and earth will pass away, but his word will not. The Church therefore reads the signs of the times under the authority of Christ, never apart from his Gospel.

Gospel: The permanence of Christ’s word gives particular weight to his teaching about vigilance. Christian watchfulness is not fearful preoccupation with catastrophe. It is the steady disposition of those who know that the crucified and risen Lord is faithful. His kingdom is near wherever his saving power judges sin, gathers the scattered, sustains the suffering, and leads his people toward the Father. The final renewal announced in Revelation is already anticipated in the life of grace, especially as the Church worships, receives the sacraments, and bears witness to the Lord. What begins now in faith will be openly manifest when God brings his work to completion.

Saints: Saint Vergilius of Salzburg offers a fitting witness to this hope in the one Creator and Savior. As an Irish monk, abbot, and later Bishop of Salzburg, he supported missionary work among Slavic peoples, encouraged learning, and contributed to the cathedral’s building. His controversy with Saint Boniface shows that real pastoral and theological disagreements can occur even among holy servants of the Gospel. The Church’s veneration of both saints does not erase those difficulties; it teaches that communion requires humility, patience, and confidence that truth belongs to God. Vergilius’s defense of the universality of God’s creation and salvation accords with the biblical vision of a renewed creation and a holy city gathered by God.

Today: These readings call believers to live with reverence before judgment and confidence in mercy. Our deeds matter, because God’s truth is not indifferent to sin or love. At the same time, the final word belongs neither to death nor to deception, but to God’s renewal. The psalm invites the Church to cultivate longing for God through worship and prayer. The Gospel asks for sober discernment, refusing both complacency and alarm. Following Saint Vergilius, the faithful may also approach questions and disagreements with patience, careful inquiry, and charity. Christ’s enduring word keeps the Church rooted in hope as she awaits the new creation God has promised.
